ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a large square divided by equally spaced horizontal and vertical lines into 4 rows and 4 columns, altogether 16 unit small squares; therefore the grid points are 5 rows and 5 columns. Reasoning: Horizontally divide the 4×4 square array into the upper two rows and the lower two rows, each part being a 2×4 strip. For any 2×4 strip, there is a horizontal grid line in the middle separating the two rows of small squares. On this dividing line there are only 5 grid points. The diagonal of any small square in the strip must have exactly one endpoint on this dividing line. Because the problem requires that any two diagonals cannot have a common point, in particular they cannot share endpoints, so within one 2×4 strip at most only 5 diagonals can be drawn. The upper and lower two 2×4 strips together have at most 5+5=10 diagonals. Attainability: Diagonals in the same direction can be drawn in the 4 small squares of the top row and the 4 small squares of the bottom row; then diagonals in the same direction can also be drawn in the leftmost small square of the second row and the rightmost small square of the third row. Thus altogether 4+4+1+1=10 diagonals are drawn, and the endpoints of these diagonals do not coincide, nor do they intersect each other. Therefore the maximum number is 10.

method.method_draft: First read the image as a 4 by 4 array of unit squares, hence a 5 by 5 lattice of grid points. Split the array horizontally into the top two rows of squares and the bottom two rows of squares. In any 2 by 4 strip, every diagonal drawn in either row of that strip has exactly one endpoint on the horizontal grid line separating the two rows of the strip. That separating line has only 5 grid points, and the text forbids any two diagonals from sharing an endpoint, so each 2 by 4 strip can contain at most 5 diagonals. Therefore the whole 4 by 4 array has at most 5 + 5 = 10 diagonals. To show 10 is attainable, draw the same-sloping diagonal in all four squares of the top row and all four squares of the bottom row, plus the same-sloping diagonal in the leftmost square of the second row and the rightmost square of the third row; these use distinct endpoints. Thus the maximum is 10.

method.method_draft: First read the image as four rows of four unit squares, with five lattice points on each boundary line between adjacent square rows. Model each possible diagonal as occupying two lattice vertices of its unit square; two choices are incompatible if they share a lattice vertex or are the two diagonals of the same square. Then solve row by row with a finite-state mask. For one row of four squares, enumerate the 3 choices in each square: no diagonal, rising diagonal, or falling diagonal, discarding row patterns that already reuse a top or bottom boundary vertex. Record each legal row pattern by a 5-bit mask of used vertices on its top boundary, a 5-bit mask of used vertices on its bottom boundary, and its number of diagonals. Combine four rows using dynamic programming: a row pattern may follow the previous row only if its top mask is disjoint from the previous bottom mask. Maximizing the total over all four rows gives 10. A maximizing pattern is: four same-sloping diagonals in row 1, one in row 2 at the far left, one in row 3 at the far right, and four in row 4.
method.CoT_raw:
Image description: The attached diagram shows a square grid made of 4 rows and 4 columns of congruent unit squares, so there are 16 unit squares total. Each horizontal boundary line of a row has 5 lattice vertices.

Reasoning by the assigned row-mask method: In each unit square there are three choices: draw no diagonal, draw the diagonal from upper-left to lower-right, or draw the diagonal from lower-left to upper-right. A chosen diagonal occupies exactly two lattice vertices. Two chosen diagonals are incompatible if they share a lattice vertex; also, only one diagonal can be chosen in a square.

For one row of 4 squares, enumerate the 3^4 possible choices. Discard row patterns that reuse a top-boundary vertex or a bottom-boundary vertex. Equivalently, adjacent nonempty squares in the same row may not have opposite-sloping diagonals, because then they share a common endpoint on their shared vertical grid line. For each legal row pattern, record three values: its 5-bit top mask, its 5-bit bottom mask, and its number of diagonals.

Now combine the four rows by dynamic programming. Let dp after a row store the best total so far for each possible bottom mask. A row pattern may be placed after a previous row only when its top mask is disjoint from the previous row's bottom mask. This exactly enforces that no diagonal endpoints are shared between adjacent rows. Since all legal row patterns are enumerated and all cross-row conflicts are checked by mask disjointness, this gives an exhaustive maximum. The finite-state computation gives maximum total 10.

A construction attaining 10 is: in the top row, draw four diagonals all from upper-left to lower-right; in row 2, draw only the far-left diagonal of the same slope; in row 3, draw only the far-right diagonal of the same slope; in the bottom row, draw four diagonals all from upper-left to lower-right. The row counts are 4 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 10, and the mask disjointness checks show no two diagonals share any endpoint.
